name: nauatl de Durango, dialecto de San Agustín de Buenaventura
confidence_why: Canger 2000, the one first-hand study of stress in San Agustín de Buenaventura, and her own 2018 summary of it agree that stress falls on the penult by default but has been drawn into the morphology so that many inflected forms carry final stress (taxkál 'tortilla' vs no-táxkal 'my tortilla', ki-tás 'he throws it' vs ki-tasá 'he threw it'), and Lastra 1981 together with the later reports of Pharao Hansen 2024, Wichmann 2024 and van der Hulst and Goedemans 2010 give the same picture, so the record rests on a single fieldworker's description with nothing against it.

catalog_quote: Me imagino que poco a poco los nauahablantes adaptaron una parte de la prosodia del español a su propio nauatl, introduciendo la pronunciación con más fuerza en la penúltima sílaba. Esto es lo que encontramos en todos los dialectos del nauatl de hoy, si bien la diferencia entre vocales largas y vocales cortas persiste en casi todos ellos. ... He encontrado la pérdida total de la duración vocálica contrastiva en un solo dialecto, el de Durango. Diré que en este dialecto la influencia ha avanzado aún más: la sílaba prominente se pronuncia más fuertemente y participa en la morfología de la misma manera que en el español, donde la reconocemos, por ejemplo, en la diferencia entre tomo y tomó. Ejemplos de este fenómeno en el nauatl de Durango serían los siguientes: taxkál (tortilla) vs no-táxkal (mi tortilla), ki-tás (lo tira) vs ki-tasá (lo tiraba).13 [fn. 13: Canger, “Stress in Nahuatl of Durango: Whose Stress?”.] ... Sabemos que hoy en día los hablantes de todos los dialectos del nauatl pronuncian sus palabras con más fuerza en la penúltima sílaba.

new_statements.translation: I have found the total loss of contrastive vowel length in only one dialect, that of Durango. I would say that in this dialect the influence has advanced even further: the prominent syllable is pronounced more strongly and takes part in the morphology in the same way as in Spanish, where we recognize it, for example, in the difference between tomo and tomó. Examples of this phenomenon in Durango Nahuatl would be the following: taxkál (tortilla) vs no-táxkal (my tortilla), ki-tás (he throws it) vs ki-tasá (he was throwing it). [...] We know that today the speakers of all Nahuatl dialects pronounce their words with more force on the penultimate syllable.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Default stress on the penultimate syllable, as in all modern Nahuatl varieties; but in the Durango (San Agustín de Buenaventura) variety, which has lost contrastive vowel length, stress has become mobile and grammatically contrastive: apocopated nouns and certain verb forms (imperfect/preterite, plural-subject -l, plural -m) carry surface final stress (taxkál vs no-táxkal; ki-tás vs ki-tasá; síwat vs siwám), and per Canger 2000 the antepenult is occasionally stressed too. Canger 2000 frames this as either (A) a penultimate default plus morphologically loaded stress rules (adverbs: final if consonant-final, penult if vowel-final; some nouns ad hoc), or (B) a phonological penultimate rule (not counting enclitics) applied before syncope of underlying word-final vowels (taxkál-me, siwá-m). The fixed: penultimate syllable label is the default rule with substantial morphological exceptions; lexical (unpredictable) would overstate it.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: Final stress on apocopated nouns and on morphologically marked verb forms (imperfect/past, plural subject) and consonant-final adverbs; occasional antepenultimate stress (Canger 2000 snippet); Canger 2000 says the raw example list 'points to no restrictions at all on stress assignment'. Canger attributes the whole pattern to Spanish influence.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (single words and inflected forms, citation and text forms); Canger 2018 speaks of 'el dialecto de Durango' generically, the data being her San Agustín de Buenaventura fieldwork (fn. 13 = Canger 2000). Canger 2000's Description B refers to enclitics not counting for the penult rule.
new_statements.identity_note: Canger's Durango data come from San Agustín de Buenaventura, Mezquital, Durango = Western Durango Nahuatl (west2778, ISO azn), which the ISO 2011-111 split also groups with Santa Cruz/Acaponeta, Nayarit. Canger 2018 says only 'el dialecto de Durango' but its fn. 13 points to Canger 2000, whose fieldwork site is San Buenaventura. The Preuss/Ziehm/Castro Medina/Reyes Taboada literature on San Pedro Jícora (Xícoras) is the sister variety Eastern Durango Nahuatl (east2695, azd), which shares the mobile-stress pattern but differs phonetically and morphologically (Reyes Taboada & Villa Reyes 2023, fn. 3). Canger 2001 (ALIM 24) covers only San Buenaventura.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's existing reading 'fixed: penultimate syllable' (from Canger 2018, which cites this chapter as its fn. 13 source): the same author's primary description keeps a basic penultimate rule but documents that in this dialect stress is morphologized and frequently final or occasionally antepenultimate, with an adverb rule and enclitic exclusion. Adds the exceptions, the morphological role and the two competing analyses; a 'penultimate' catalog entry for west2778 should carry a note that surface stress is not phonologically predictable here.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default stress on the penultimate syllable (enclitics not counted), but in San Agustín de Buenaventura the pattern is 'less stable' than in other Nahuatl: surface stress can be final (kitasalá 'he threw it', kinán 'how?', taxkál 'tortilla') or occasionally antepenultimate, and Canger says the example list 'points to no restrictions at all on stress assignment'. She gives two sketches: Description A treats stress as part of the morphology (basic penult rule A; rules with high functional load tied to nominal and verbal inflection B; adverb rule C: final stress if the adverb ends in a consonant, penultimate if it ends in a vowel; D an ad hoc observation that some words, particularly nouns, do not conform); Description B is purely phonological (penult not counting enclitics, plus vowel syncope of final vowels and underlying vowels, so taxkál < taxkal(i), siwá-m 'women'). The title's question ('whose stress?') concerns whether the innovation is due to Spanish contact.

new_statements.exceptions: final stress in many verb forms with morphological load (e.g. kitasalá 'he threw it' imperfect vs present penult forms; kitasaskiá 'he would throw it'), in consonant-final nouns after final-vowel syncope (taxkál 'tortilla', siwá-m 'women', plural taxkál-me), in consonant-final adverbs; occasional antepenultimate stress (itokáloha 'they may be named' in the earlier harvest); 'some words, particularly nouns, do not' follow the rules (ad hoc list D); enclitics excluded from the count
new_statements.identity_note: Canger 2000 describes the Nahuatl of San Agustín de Buenaventura, Durango (fieldwork 1993, 1995, 1996), which is exactly west2778 (Western Durango Nahuatl / mexicanero). The chapter also draws on Preuss's 1905-1907 texts from San Pedro Jícora (east2695), but the stress description is for San Buenaventura.

new_statements.rule_in_words: San Agustín de Buenaventura (Durango) Nahuatl: penultimate stress is the unmarked/default pattern, but surface stress is not mechanically predictable. Description A (morphological): default penult; final stress marks grammatical categories (class-1 nouns in -l stressed finally when unpossessed, taxkál, vs penult when possessed, no-táxkal; class-2/3 nouns final-stressed in the plural, siwá-m vs síwa-t; in verbs 'imperfect' -a and 'hypo 2' -skiá attract stress, wé¢ka 'he laughs' vs we¢ká 'he laughed'; 'hypo 1' gives antepenult stress); adverbs take final stress if consonant-final, penult if vowel-final; some words (esp. nouns, loans like mayrón, beldúk) must be lexically marked. Description B (purely phonological): one rule, stress on the penult not counting enclitics, computed on longer underlying forms whose final vowels are optionally syncopated (taxkál[i], siwá-m[e]), plus lexically marked exceptions. In connected speech over a third of polysyllabic words carry final stress (72/180 in one text). Author attributes the innovative pattern to Spanish influence (section 6). Contrastive vowel length plays no role in the account.
new_statements.secondary_stress: nothing said about secondary stress (no mention anywhere in the chapter).
new_statements.exceptions: vocative final stress in Classical Nahuatl (obsolete); Durango: final stress on unpossessed class-1 nouns in -l and on plural nouns of classes 2-3; final stress on imperfect/perfect-type verb forms (-a 'imperfect', -skiá 'hypo 2'); antepenult stress with -ha 'hypo 1' (analysed as an enclitic in Description B); adverbs: final if consonant-final (akán?, k(i)yawah etc.), penult if vowel-final; class-4 nouns and loans with no pattern (péloh, mayrón 'madrone', beldúk 'knife', abyón) marked individually; enclitics (-ha, -ke plural subject in some analyses) not counted.
new_statements.identity_note: The chapter describes the Nahuatl of San Agustín de Buenaventura, Durango ('Sanbueneros'), with a brief interview from San Pedro Jícora and Preuss's 1905-07 texts from San Pedro Jícora as background; San Agustín de Buenaventura is exactly the variety named by west2778 (Western Durango Nahuatl / mexicanero).

readall_conflicts: No disagreement between sources. Canger 2000 (primary, snippets) and Canger 2018 (already in the catalog) both give a basic penultimate rule for San Agustín de Buenaventura while stating that stress there has been pulled into the morphology and often falls on the final (occasionally antepenultimate) syllable; the second-hand summaries held by the project (Pharao Hansen 2024, Wichmann ed. 2024, van der Hulst & Goedemans 2010, Hernández de León-Portilla 2007, Lastra 1981 snippet 'regular pattern' aténko, méste, kámak) say the same. The only tension is internal to Canger 2000: her own sentence that the example list 'points to no restrictions at all on stress assignment' versus her rule A (penult by default); she resolves it by treating the departures as morphological or as the result of final-vowel syncope, so a catalog reader should treat 'penultimate' as the default, not as a surface generalization.
